470.title: Dhul-Qarnayn's wall
470.hook: a just king builds a barrier of iron and copper for a people and calls it a mercy (18:83–98)
470.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Dhul-Qarnayn as a model of just rule: power used to protect the weak, without payment, and credited to God; scholars have long debated his identity without agreement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boat, the boy and the wall, and your line was there was a reason. When something went wrong, did you wait before deciding what it meant? Day four hundred seventy, our last day in al-Kahf.

The last story in al-Kahf starts with a question people put to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: tell us about Dhul-Qarnayn. The name means the one with two horns, or the man of two ages, or of two ends of the earth; the commentators offer several. He's a ruler given power and the means to use it. He travels to where the sun sets, then to where it rises, and then to a pass between two mountains, where a frightened people are waiting for him.

The people at the pass, the surah says, could hardly understand speech. But they manage to say it: Ya'juj and Ma'juj, Gog and Magog, are ruining the land. Will you build a barrier between us and them if we pay you? Dhul-Qarnayn turns the money down. What my Lord has given me is better, he says. Help me with your strength instead. Bring me blocks of iron. They stack the iron until it fills the gap between the two mountainsides. Then he says: blow, and they work the bellows until the iron glows like fire. Then: bring me molten copper to pour over it. And the wall holds. The surah says the raiders could neither climb it nor dig through it. Now the line this day is built on. Standing in front of the thing he built, he says, in Pickthall's words: "This is a mercy from my Lord". And then: when my Lord's promise comes, He will level it to the ground, and my Lord's promise is true. Earlier in this same surah, a man walked through his gardens saying this will never perish. Here a man stands before iron and copper and says: it's a mercy, and it will fall when God decides. Who was Dhul-Qarnayn? Muslim scholars have long disagreed. Some said Alexander the Great, some Cyrus of Persia, some an ancient king of Yemen. The Qur'an doesn't say. What it tells is what he did with power: he refused payment, put people to work on their own protection, and gave the credit away. In the modern four-trials reading we met on Friday, that completes the set: faith in the cave, wealth in the garden, knowledge by the sea, and power at the wall.
screen: `GOG AND MAGOG AT THE PASS.` · `NO PAYMENT. HELP ME WITH STRENGTH.` · `IRON, FIRE, MOLTEN COPPER.` · `IT WILL FALL WHEN GOD DECIDES.` · then, large: `THIS IS A MERCY FROM MY LORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who needs protecting: a child, an aging parent, a coworker being worn down, yourself. What's the gap their trouble gets in through? Late nights, a bad influence, money stress, a person who won't stop calling. Picture one small barrier you could help build with them, not for them: a bedtime, a budget, a boundary, a lock that works. Picture handing the credit away when it holds. The bell holds the time.
Dhul-Qarnayn's wall. Iron and molten copper across a mountain pass, built with the people's own hands, and called a mercy from God. Today's word.
Your line: a mercy from my lord. Today, build one small protective thing, and when it works, say whose mercy it was. Day four hundred seventy.

what it means: a ruler used power to protect the weak, refused payment, worked alongside them, and credited God.
what a scholar hears: qarn means both horn and age; his identity is debated (Alexander, Cyrus, a Himyarite king), and the Qur'an's silence on it is often noted.

471.title: A call in secret
471.hook: Zakariyya's bones are weak and hair white, but he's never been disappointed in prayer (19:3–4)
471.howItsDone: Many Muslims make private du'a, often at night, for long-held wishes such as children, and cite Zakariyya's prayer in 19:3–6 and 21:89 as a model of quiet persistence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dhul-Qarnayn's wall, and your line was a mercy from my Lord. Did you build one small protective thing? Day four hundred seventy-one, and a new surah.

Surah nineteen is named for a woman: Maryam, the mother of 'Isa. She is the only woman the Qur'an names, and this surah carries her name on the cover. But it doesn't open with her. It opens with an old man, alone, at night, praying so quietly that nobody else could hear. He's been asking for the same thing for years. Today: his prayer, and the sentence in it that has kept people asking ever since.

The old man is Zakariyya, Zechariah, a guardian of the temple and of the young Maryam. In Pickthall's words, the surah calls this a mention of God's mercy to His servant, "When he cried unto his Lord a cry in secret". Nida'an khafiyya: a hidden call. Why hidden? Commentators have suggested several reasons: humility, or the late hour, or that he was embarrassed to ask, at his age, for a child. Then he describes himself, with complete honesty: my bones have grown weak, and my head is ablaze with white hair. And then he says this, in Pickthall's words: "and I have never been unblest in prayer to Thee, my Lord." Look at the logic. He doesn't say: I've always gotten what I asked for. He says: I've never come away from asking You empty, never been left wretched by it. His case for asking again isn't his strength, which is gone, or his wife's, who has never had a child. It's his history with God. Asking has always been good for him, so he asks. He asks for an heir, someone to carry on the family of Ya'qub. And the answer comes: a son, named Yahya, a name, the surah says, given to no one before him. When Zakariyya asks for a sign, he's told he won't speak to people for three nights, though nothing is wrong with him. A man who prayed in secret is given silence. There's a hadith in Muslim's collection that sits beside this: a person's prayer is answered as long as they don't grow impatient and say, I prayed and prayed and saw nothing, and give up.
screen: `ZAKARIYYA, OLD, AT NIGHT.` · `NIDA'AN KHAFIYYA: A HIDDEN CALL.` · `HIS CASE: HIS HISTORY WITH GOD.` · `A SON, AND THREE NIGHTS OF SILENCE.` · then, large: `I HAVE NEVER BEEN UNBLEST IN PRAYER TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Think of an old wish, something you asked for once, maybe years ago, and stopped asking for because nothing seemed to happen. Let it come back without embarrassment. If you pray, you can ask for it again, quietly, the way Zakariyya did, in your own words. You might begin as he did, with honesty about where you are. If you don't pray, just hold the wish and notice whether you'd given up on it, and whether you want to. The bell holds the time.
A call in secret. Zakariyya's quiet prayer at night, old and honest, built on one fact: asking had never left him empty. Today's word.
Your line: never disappointed in asking. Today, ask for one thing you'd stopped asking for, from God if you pray, or from a person if that's who can help. Day four hundred seventy-one.

472.title: Yahya, gentle
472.hook: Yahya is given wisdom as a child and is dutiful and gentle to his parents (19:12–15)
472.howItsDone: Muslims honor Yahya as a prophet and son of Zakariyya; his portrait in 19:12–15 is often taught to young people as a model of wisdom joined with gentleness toward parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a call in secret: Zakariyya, old, asking again. Your line was never disappointed in asking. Did you ask for something you'd stopped asking for? Day four hundred seventy-two.

A child an old couple waited years for. You might expect him to be spoiled: every wish granted, every tantrum forgiven, the center of a house that had been quiet a long time. The Qur'an gives us that child: the son of Zakariyya, the answer to the secret call. And in four short verses it describes who he grew up to be. It's almost the opposite of spoiled. Today: Yahya.

Christians know him as John the Baptist. In the Qur'an he's Yahya, and Surah Maryam gives him a short portrait. Verse twelve: he's told to hold fast to the scripture, and given hukm, wisdom, judgment, while still a child. Verse thirteen: and hanan from Us, and purity, and he was mindful of God. Hanan is tenderness, the softness of compassion, and it's described as coming from God's own presence. Then verse fourteen, in Pickthall's words: "And dutiful toward his parents. And he was not arrogant, rebellious." Barr, dutiful: it's the same root as birr al-walidayn, the name Muslims give to the goodness to parents that Al-Isra commands. And the two things he wasn't: jabbar, overbearing, someone who forces his will on others, and 'asiyy, disobedient. Notice what's being praised. A boy given wisdom early could easily have become proud of it, the kid who knows better than his old parents. Instead the portrait puts wisdom and tenderness side by side, and the gentleness lands on the people closest to him, the father and mother who'd waited so long. Then verse fifteen gives him a blessing that marks the three great thresholds of a life: "Peace on him the day he was born, and the day he dieth and the day he shall be raised alive!" Born, dying, raised. A few verses later in this same surah, 'Isa, his cousin in the tradition, says nearly the same words about himself. Two prophets, side by side, each wrapped in peace from beginning to end. And Yahya's portrait begins in the home: wise, tender, dutiful, and not proud.
screen: `HUKM: WISDOM AS A CHILD.` · `HANAN: TENDERNESS FROM GOD.` · `DUTIFUL, NOT OVERBEARING.` · `PEACE AT BIRTH, DEATH, AND RISING.` · then, large: `GENTLE, NOT PROUD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one of your parents, or someone who did a parent's work for you. Bring to mind the last time you were impatient with them: corrected them, rolled your eyes, explained something too fast. No guilt, just look. Now picture the same moment done Yahya's way: you still know what you know, but you say it softly, and you let them keep their dignity. If they've died, you can let this be a memory you hold gently. The bell holds the time.
Yahya. The long-awaited son, wise as a child, tender, dutiful to his parents, not overbearing, and given peace on every threshold of his life. Today's word.
Your line: gentle, not proud. Today, the next time you know better than a parent or an older person, say it gently, or don't say it at all. Day four hundred seventy-two.

473.title: "O my father"
473.hook: Ibrahim pleads with his father gently four times, and parts with, peace be upon you (19:41–47)
473.howItsDone: Muslim teachers cite Ibrahim's words in 19:42–47 as the model for speaking to parents who don't share one's faith: gently, respectfully, and without abandoning conviction.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yahya: wise as a child, tender to his parents. Your line was gentle, not proud. Did you say something gently to an older person, or let it go? Day four hundred seventy-three.

Politics at the holiday table. A career. A marriage. Faith. An argument with a parent about something that matters can start calm and end with someone leaving the room. Surah Maryam has one of these conversations, between a young man and his father, and the subject is God. It starts calm. It ends badly. But the way the son leaves the room is the whole lesson. Listen, too, for how he begins each sentence.

The son is Ibrahim. His father, named Azar in another surah, makes and serves idols. And Ibrahim begins each of his four sentences the same way: ya abati. O my father. Grammarians note that this form of address is a tender one, something like my dear father. One: my father, why worship what can't hear, can't see, and can't help you at all? Two: my father, knowledge has come to me that hasn't come to you, so follow me, and I'll guide you on a level road. Three: my father, don't serve Shaytan. Four: my father, I'm afraid a punishment from the Merciful will touch you. Notice that the fourth isn't a threat. It's fear for him. Then the father answers. Do you turn away from my gods, Ibrahim? If you don't stop, I'll stone you. Get away from me for a long time. Plenty of arguments end right there. Ibrahim's reply, in Pickthall's words, begins: "Peace be unto thee!" Salamun 'alayk. Then: I'll ask my Lord to forgive you; He has always been kind to me. And: I'll withdraw from you and from what you call on, and I'll call on my Lord. He leaves, and he doesn't slam the door. He doesn't give up his conviction either. Both are true at once. The Qur'an is honest that the story goes further: another surah, At-Tawbah, says that later, when it became clear his father was set against God, Ibrahim dissociated himself from him. But in this moment, threatened with stoning, he answers with peace, and a promise to pray.
screen: `YA ABATI: MY DEAR FATHER.` · `FOUR PLEAS, THE LAST ONE FEAR.` · `I'LL STONE YOU. GET AWAY FROM ME.` · `SALAMUN 'ALAYK.` · then, large: `PEACE BE UNTO THEE!`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a disagreement you're in with someone close: a parent, a sibling, an old friend. Picture the last time it came up, and how it ended. Now picture yourself at the end of that conversation doing what Ibrahim did: keeping your view, and still leaving with peace. What would you actually say? Peace be with you. I'll keep you in my prayers. I love you, and I see it differently. Find the words that are yours. The bell holds the time.
O my father. Ya abati: Ibrahim's tender address, four times, to a father who threatened him, ending with peace. Today's word.
Your line: peace be upon you, father. Today, leave one disagreement with peace: keep your view, and end with a kind word instead of a final one. Day four hundred seventy-three.

474.title: Love appointed
474.hook: the Merciful will appoint love for those who believe and do good (19:96)
474.howItsDone: Muslims cite 19:96 and the hadith of Jibril's call when speaking of the love people feel for the righteous; teachers emphasize doing good sincerely, for God, rather than to be admired.

segments.voice: Yesterday, O my father: Ibrahim's four gentle pleas, and a parting with peace. Did you leave a disagreement with a kind word? Day four hundred seventy-four, our last day in Surah Maryam.
screen: `O MY FATHER — PEACE BE UPON YOU.`

segments.voice: Some people are like this: not the loudest at the party, not the most famous, not the one working hardest to be liked. And yet when their name comes up, faces soften. Neighbors bring them soup when they're sick. Their funeral, when it comes, is full. Nobody can quite say how it happened. Near the very end of Surah Maryam there's a verse that names what happened, and says who did it.

Verse ninety-six, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! those who believe and do good works, the Beneficent will appoint for them love." The Beneficent is ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful, a name of God that comes back again and again in Surah Maryam. The word for love is wudd: warm, steady affection, the kind that lasts. It shares its root with one of God's names, al-Wadud, the Loving. And the verb is sa-yaj'alu: He will make, He will place, He will appoint. Love isn't earned here like a wage, or chased like a prize. It's placed, by God, in hearts. Commentators asked: whose hearts? Some said: in the hearts of other people, so that the good are loved by those around them. Some said: between the believers themselves. Some said: God's own love for them. The Arabic leaves room for all three. And a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim draws the picture. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: when God loves a servant, He calls Jibril and says, I love this person, so love them. And Jibril loves them. Then Jibril calls out to the people of heaven: God loves this person, so love them. And the people of heaven love them. Then acceptance is placed for them on earth. Notice the order. It starts in heaven and arrives on earth last. The neighbor bringing soup is the end of a long chain. Notice also what the verse asks of people: believe, and do good. It doesn't say: try to be liked. This surah opened with Zakariyya calling in secret, then Yahya's tenderness, Ibrahim's peace toward his father. It closes with this: love that is given, not grabbed.
screen: `AR-RAHMAN WILL APPOINT.` · `WUDD: WARM, STEADY LOVE.` · `JIBRIL, THEN HEAVEN, THEN EARTH.` · `BELIEVE AND DO GOOD. NOT: BE LIKED.` · then, large: `THE BENEFICENT WILL APPOINT FOR THEM LOVE.`

segments.voice: Choose one good thing you could do today that no one will see or thank you for. Taking out a neighbor's bins. Paying for someone's coffee and leaving before they notice. If you pray, praying for someone who's unkind to you. Picture yourself doing it, and picture walking away without telling anyone. Notice the small pull to be seen. Let it go. Leave the love, if it comes, for God to place. The bell holds the time.
Love appointed. Wudd, warm and lasting love, placed by the Most Merciful for those who believe and do good. Today's word.
Your line: love will be appointed. Today, do one good thing quietly, and don't tell anyone about it, not even later. Day four hundred seventy-four.

475.title: Not to distress you
475.hook: We did not send the Qur'an to make you miserable (20:2)
475.howItsDone: Muslim teachers cite 20:2, 2:185 and the hadith 'the religion is ease' to warn against making religion a burden; Taha is also used as a given name, from the opening letters of this surah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, love appointed, and your line was love will be appointed. Did you do one good thing and keep it to yourself? Day four hundred seventy-five, and a new surah.

Some people carry their faith like a backpack full of stones. Every missed prayer is a stone. Every slip is a stone. They're trying so hard that the thing meant to hold them up is wearing them down. If that's ever been you, or someone you love, Surah twenty has something to say before it says anything else. It opens with two Arabic letters, and then, in its very first sentence, it tells the Prophet what the Qur'an is not for.

The two letters are Ta and Ha. Like the other letters that open some surahs, their meaning is debated. Some read Ta-Ha as a name for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and Taha is given as a boy's name for that reason. Others said it means O man, in an old dialect. Others simply said: God knows best. Then verse two, in Pickthall's words: "We have not revealed unto thee (Muhammad) this Qur'an that thou shouldst be distressed". The word is tashqa: to be wretched, worn out, miserable. It shares a root with the word Zakariyya used in Surah Maryam: I have never been left wretched in my prayer to You. Two surahs in a row, the same root: a man never left wretched by prayer, and a Qur'an not sent to make anyone wretched. Commentators give reasons for the verse. One report says the Prophet stood in night prayer so long his feet swelled. Another says his opponents mocked him: this Qur'an has made you miserable. The verse answers both. Verse three says what the Qur'an is for: a reminder, for whoever stands in awe. A hadith in Bukhari puts it plainly: the religion is ease, and nobody makes it hard on themselves except that it overcomes them. So aim for what's right, come close to it, and be of good cheer. This doesn't mean faith asks nothing. Ta-Ha goes on to tell the long story of Musa, which is anything but easy. But it begins by saying what the weight is for. Not misery. Reminder. The stones in the backpack were never the point.

segments.voice: Sit, and notice if there's anything you're carrying about your faith, or about trying to be a good person, that feels like a stone: a guilt, a standard you never meet, a practice you dread. Name it to yourself. Now ask: what was this meant to be for? Remembering? Rest? Connection? If you pray, you can ask for ease in it. If not, just let the stone sit down beside you for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Not to distress you. The opening promise of Ta-Ha: the Qur'an wasn't sent to wear anyone out, but as a reminder. Today's word.
Your line: not to distress you. Today, let your faith, or whatever you hold sacred, lighten you once: do the part that gives you rest, and do it gladly. Day four hundred seventy-five.

476.title: Umar hears Ta-Ha
476.hook: on his way to harm the Prophet ﷺ, Umar reads Ta-Ha at his sister's house and is changed
476.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Umar's conversion from the sirah literature as an example of the Qur'an's power to move a hostile heart; many also honor his sister Fatima's courage in the account.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the opening of Ta-Ha, and your line was not to distress you. Did something sacred lighten you, even once? Day four hundred seventy-six, the end of a week.

Mecca, some years after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ began to preach. A tall, hot-tempered man named Umar ibn al-Khattab is walking fast through the streets with a sword. He's decided the new religion has divided his city long enough, and he's going to end it by killing the man who brought it. On the way, someone stops him and says: before you fix other people's families, look at your own. Your sister has become a Muslim.

This story comes from Ibn Ishaq's biography of the Prophet. It isn't in the Qur'an or in Bukhari or Muslim, and the sources tell it with variations, but it's one of the best-loved conversion stories in Muslim memory. Here's how Ibn Ishaq tells it. Umar turns around and goes to his sister Fatima's house. Inside, she and her husband Sa'id are being taught by a companion named Khabbab, reading from a page. They hear Umar coming and hide the page. He bursts in: what was that murmuring I heard? He grabs his brother-in-law, and when his sister steps between them, he strikes her and she bleeds. And she says to his face: yes, we're Muslims. Do what you like. Seeing her blood, Umar is ashamed. He asks for the page. She says: you're not clean; wash first. He washes. And he reads the opening of Ta-Ha: the verses we read yesterday, We did not send down the Qur'an to distress you, but as a reminder. When he finished, the report says, he said: how beautiful, how noble these words are. Khabbab comes out of hiding. Umar asks where the Prophet is, goes to the house where the Muslims were meeting, and declares his faith. The man who set out to end the religion became one of its pillars, and later the second caliph. Notice what changed him. Not an argument, not a miracle, not a threat. His sister's courage, and a page of words read slowly. This week ran from Dhul-Qarnayn's wall through Zakariyya's secret call, Yahya's gentleness, Ibrahim's peace toward his father, love appointed, and Ta-Ha's promise. And it ends on a page in a sister's hands.

segments.voice: Think of a page that once changed you. A verse, a poem, a letter from someone, a paragraph in a book, a line a teacher wrote in the margin. Try to remember where you were when you first read it, and what shifted. If you can find it today, plan to reread it slowly. If you can't, sit with whatever words of it you still carry, and let them do their work again. The bell holds the time.
Umar hears Ta-Ha. A man with a sword, a sister who wouldn't hide, and the opening of a surah read slowly enough to change him. Today's word.
Your line: the page changed him. Today, reread something that once changed you, and notice what it says to you now. Day four hundred seventy-six.
